events.title: The EU Environmental Crime Directive: a new step in the fight for environmental justice
events.description: Criminal law is an important tool to protect the environment and advance environmental justice. EU member states including the Netherlands are working on legislation to implement the new EU Environmental Crime Directive (ECD). Civil society has a key but sometimes overlooked role to play in ensuring environmental criminal law is effectively enforced to protect both the communities affected by environmental crime and the ecosystems at the heart of climate and environmental action. ThisThe EU Environmental Crime Directive: a new step in the fight for environmental justicroundtable invites participants to reflect on how environmental crime is addressed in the Netherlands, what the ECD aims to strengthen or change, and opportunities it offers for civil society actors working on environmental protection.

events.title: Blue on the beauty of De Stijl and the strength of NATO - Exhibit
events.description: Visit an intriguing exhibition at Kunstmuseum Den Haag about aesthetics and politics, focusing  on the visual identity of NATO and modern art by Piet Mondrian, Gerrit Rietveld and artists.

events.title:
Justice and Redress for Survivors of Conflict-Related Sexual Violence at the International Court of Justice.

Panel 1 — Redress for Survivors at the ICJ: Implementation of the DRC v. Uganda Reparations Order
events.description:
During The Hague Justice Week the Dr. Denis Mukwege Foundation will convene three expert panel discussions confronting a question survivors of conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV) force us to ask honestly: does international law, and the international justice system built to enforce it, actually change survivors’ lives in practice?  

In panel 1 experts will examine whether Congolese victims and communities have received the compensation the Court intended, and the role of victims, civil society, and the international community in ensuring tangible redress.

events.title: Justice as Critical Infrastructure for Peace and Resilience
events.host: International IDEA, Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL)
events.description: The event will explore how justice systems and institutions become part of the infrastructure through which societies rebuild trust, resilience and stability. The session will move beyond the narrow scope of formal courts and legal institutions and consider the wider justice ecosystem and how legal and governance frameworks can better connect with people's everyday realities.

events.title: Justice in wartime: How Ukraine is building accountability during war
events.host: International Development Law Organisation (IDLO), T.M.Asser Institute, Center for International Legal Cooperation (CILC), the Netherlands Helsinki Committee (NHC), The Embassy of Ukraine to The Netherlands and The Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs
events.description:
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has given rise to widespread international crimes and created one of the largest accountability challenges in recent history. Ukraine's Office of the Prosecutor General (OPG) has now registered more than 260,000 alleged war crimes — from attacks against civilians and conflict-related sexual violence to enforced disappearance and the deportation of children.
Ukraine's prosecutors, investigators, defence lawyers, and judges continue to investigate and adjudicate alleged atrocities under active-conflict conditions, with constrained resources and sustained pressure. Their work is complemented by civil-society organizations documenting violations and supporting survivors. Drawing on the consortium programme implemented by IDLO with Asser, CILC and NHC, the session will examine Ukraine's national accountability efforts, including legal reform, prosecution strategy, judicial capacity, victim and witness protection, and the place of veterans in the justice system. Ukrainian practitioners and policymakers will join international experts and civil-society representatives to consider progress, remaining gaps and priorities for sustaining credible and nationally led accountability efforts.

events.title:
Justice and Redress for Survivors of Conflict-Related Sexual Violence at the International Court of Justice.  

Panel 2 — Justice for Survivors at the ICJ: The Gambia v. Myanmar Case
events.description:
During The Hague Justice Week  the Dr. Denis Mukwege Foundation will convene three expert panel discussions confronting a question survivors of conflict-related sexual violence  force us to ask honestly: does international law, and the international justice system built to enforce it, actually change survivors’ lives in practice? Not as an abstract legal question, but as a tangible reality for survivors in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar, and throughout the world — people whose pain has continued for years, and whose right to justice has been delayed even longer.

With judgment expected in late 2026 in The Gambia v. Myanmar Case, this panel explores the legal significance of  conflict-related sexual violence as an underlying act of genocide, survivors’ own expectations of justice, and whether the case can advance peace amid Myanmar’s ongoing civil war.

events.title: International Justice and the Digital Realm: Addressing the Legislative and Adjudicative Gaps
events.host: ProtectNGO, Embassy of The Kingdom of The Netherlands, and City of The Hague
events.description:
In 2026, the International Court of Justice celebrates its 80th anniversary . Founded in the aftermath of World War II, the ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations. To honour this anniversary year , the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in London, in partnership with the City of The Hague and Protect.ngo, is pleased to organise a high-level discussion on “International Justice and the Digital Realm: Addressing the
Legislative and Adjudicative Gaps.” This discussion takes place under the broader anniversary theme “Peace through Law: 80 Years and Beyond.” 
As challenges to accountability in cyberspace continue to grow , senior experts from government, civil society , academia, philanthropy , and the technical community will come together to examine two key dimensions: 
- First, how digital harms and cyber operations expose gaps in international law and adjudication, including questions of attribution, evidence, and state responsibility; 
- Second, how technical evidence can be translated into legally actionable material, and what institutional, operational, and cooperative mechanisms are needed to support accountability in international fora such as the ICJ.

Participants will explore how emerging initiatives, including H-ARMOR, can contribute to international accountability by transforming technical findings into legally usable material and facilitating information sharing and attribution.

events.title: Bridging the Gap, Renewing the Promise:  International law and Global Solidarity in the Palestinian Quest for Justice
events.host: Council of Arab Ambassadors & Legal Mobilisation Platform at the International Institute of Social Studies
events.venue: International Institute of Social Studies (ISS), Kortenaerkade 12, 2518 AX Den Haag
events.description:
International law has long held out the promise of peace and justice for the Palestinian people. Yet the gap between that promise and its implementation remains uneven across nations, what some commentators have referred to as “Justice for Some”. This event examines that gap not as a story of failure alone but as a call to renew the commitment that international law represents, namely, that no people shall be denied self-determination, protection, and recourse to justice.

Palestine’s recourse to justice under international law reveals both the possibilities and the challenges inherent in the promise of peace and justice that international law represents and which global solidarity efforts seek to amplify and mobilize. Despite several legal determinations on the Question of Palestine achieved in recent years, such as three landmark Advisory Opinions of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 2004, 2024 and 2025, inter alia, that reaffirmed the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, protection from prolonged occupation, and the illegality of Israel’s occupation, and solidarity actions, the failure to implement is jarring. 

In spite of what international law has already committed regarding Palestine, trust in international law and the law-based international order has been undermined. To restore faith generally in the effectiveness of international law and enforcement institutions, as vividly illustrated regarding the Question of Palestine, the gap between the legal framework and its enforcement must be bridged.

Join us this evening to listen to legal experts and figures of authority in international law who will address this gap and share with us their insights on how we can restore the faith in international law. A Q&A will follow the panel.

events.title: International Law as a Compass for Foreign Policy
events.host: Advisory Committee on Public International Law (CAVV)
events.description:
In this session members of the CAVV will present their thoughts on the role of international law in foreign policy and focus on Dutch foreign policy. They will discuss how the Netherlands has always been a proponent of international law and, as a result, The Hague has developed into the capital of Peace and Justice. 

The panel will discuss the following questions: how do current geopolitical developments affect or even threaten the rule-based order and how does The Netherlands position itself in this context? 

The panel is organised in a town hall debate-format where panel members will give short pitches/introductions and actively engage with questions from a lay and expert audience. We hope to achieve an informed and stimulating debate on the current state of international law and how it impacts the position of the Netherlands and The Hague as capital of peace and justice.

events.title: Making Human Rights Law Work: Building new alliances between business, finance & civil society
events.host: European Center for Non-Profit Law (ECNL), ABN AMRO
events.description: Human rights and environmental due diligence laws increasingly require companies and financial institutions to identify, prevent and address adverse human rights impacts. Effective implementation depends on access to reliable, independent information from civil society organisations, journalists, trade unions, researchers and affected communities. However, as civic space faces growing restrictions worldwide, this vital information ecosystem is becoming more vulnerable. This session examines why shrinking civic space is not only a civil society issue, but also a business, banking and justice concern. Bringing together representatives from business, finance, civil society and policy, it will highlight practical examples of cross-sector collaboration, including the Dutch KYC (Know Your Customer) standard to reduce NGO de-risking and research on conducting human rights due diligence in restrictive contexts. Participants will explore how new partnerships can strengthen accountability and help translate human rights laws into effective practice.

events.title: Heritage on Trial: Can International Law Still Protect What War Destroys?
events.host: Embassy of Ukraine in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Embassy of the United Kingdom
events.description:
Heritage on Trial: Can International Law Still Protect What War Destroys?

When a museum is shelled, a church burned, or a collection looted in wartime, is it simply a tragedy — or a crime that someone can be held to account for? Russia’s war against Ukraine has damaged, destroyed or emptied hundreds of museums, churches, libraries and archives, and cultural objects have been carried out of occupied territory. This has turned a long-standing legal promise — that cultural heritage must be protected even in war — into one of its hardest real-world tests.
This expert discussion brings together people who work on that promise from every side: Ukrainian officials and cultural first responders documenting the damage, international prosecutors and judges, and legal scholars. Together they will ask what the law can and cannot yet do — from the 1954 Hague Convention (the main treaty protecting cultural property in war) to the first international conviction for destroying heritage, and the mechanisms for recovering stolen objects.

Participants can expect a frank, accessible conversation — no legal background needed — about where protection works, where it fails, and what needs to change.
Why attend? Because the questions raised in Ukraine will shape how the world protects culture in every future conflict. The Hague, as the city of international law and justice, is where that conversation belongs

events.title: Historic The Hague: The Origins of the City of Peace and Justice
events.venue: City Hall (Spui 70), in front of The Hague International Centre (THIC)
events.description: This 2-hour walking tour takes you back in time, revealing how The Hague grew into the international City of Peace and Justice, while maintaining its long-standing role as the political heart of the Netherlands. As you stroll through historic streets and past iconic landmarks, you will uncover the stories that connect the city's national and international significance.

events.title:
Justice and Redress for Survivors of Conflict-Related Sexual Violence at the International Court of Justice.

Panel 3 — Beyond the Courtroom: Survivor-Led Advocacy and the Future of Justice for Conflict-Related Sexual Violence (Closing Panel)
events.description:
During The Hague Justice Week the Dr. Denis Mukwege Foundation will convene three expert panel discussions confronting a question survivors of conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV) force us to ask honestly: does international law, and the international justice system built to enforce it, actually change survivors’ lives in practice? Not as an abstract legal question, but as a tangible reality for survivors in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar, and throughout the world — people whose pain has continued for years, and whose right to justice has been delayed even longer.    

Closing The Hague Justice Week, this panel draws together the findings of the DRC v. Uganda and Gambia v. Myanmar panels to ask what comes next. It spotlights the Mukwege Foundation’s and SEMA’s tools for translating legal obligations into survivor-centred practice — including the Guidebook on State Obligations for Conflict-Related Sexual Violence and SEMA’s Call to Action — and considers what “80 years and beyond” of international law must look like if it is to deliver, in practice as much as in principle, on its promise to survivors.

events.title: Justice has no Passport: A Global Conversation on Universal Jurisdiction
events.description:
A virtual conversation on universal jurisdiction. One of the most powerful, yet still underused and often misunderstood, tools for holding perpetrators of the world’s gravest crimes accountable.
Bringing together speakers with diverse regional and professional perspectives, the discussion will explore how universal jurisdiction has evolved, the challenges it faces today, and the role it can play in advancing accountability and international justice in a global order under increasing strain.
The conversation is open to anyone interested in the fight against impunity and the future of international justice—including legal professionals, students, policymakers, and civil society actors.
At a time when the international justice system is facing unprecedented pressure, this session offers an opportunity to hear directly from practitioners working across different contexts to strengthen universal jurisdiction and renew its promise as a tool for justice.

Meet the Speakers:

- Tomas Kevin Manguel, Professor of International Criminal Law at the University of Buenos Aires and Legal Adviser at StraLi

- Marie Wilmet, Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellow, Université libre de Bruxelles

- Atilla Kisla, Human rights lawyer, International Justice Cluster Lead at Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)

- Priya Pillai, PhD, International lawyer, and executive director of the Asia Justice Coalition

The session will be moderated by Alessia Schiavon, Executive Director FIBGAR

events.title: Mapping the Gaps in International Law: Introducing the OLJA International Law Gap Report
events.description:
International law promises protection and accountability, but too often its rules are weak, unclear or simply not enforced. This session introduces the International Law Gap Report, a research project by Omnijuris Law & Justice Advocates (OLJA) that maps where international humanitarian law, human rights law, international criminal law and refugee law fall short in practice, and where reform could close the gap.

The OLJA team will present the report's approach and first findings, followed by an open discussion with the audience. No specialist knowledge is needed, and technical terms will be explained.

Join us to learn how the report was built, share your own experience of where the law falls short, and find out how to contribute to the next stage of the project.

events.title: The ICJ at 100: Realistic Expectations on the World Court’s Next 20 Years
events.description: The ICJ at 100: Realistic Expectations on the World Court’s next 20 Years will have a mixture of legal advisers and counsel who regularly appear before the ICJ. The panellists will discuss their unique perspectives on the current challenges facing the Court, as well as considering what we can realistically expect from the Court’s next 20 years. Will the Court play an even more central role in international affairs? Is it likely to be the victim of backlash or neglect? Will there be a World Court at all? Panellists will reflect on such questions, and engage with questions from attendees.

events.title: From Ukraine to Global Accountability: Presenting the Manual on Prosecuting International Environmental Crimes
events.host: Embassy of Ukraine in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Climate Counsel and UCLA Promise Institute for Human Rights
events.description:
Wars have environmental consequences, and they have long been among the least prosecuted. Nature reserves and national parks destroyed, forests burned, soil and water contaminated, biodiversity lost: damage that outlasts the fighting by decades and almost never reaches a courtroom. Ukraine has begun to change that.

Under war conditions, Ukrainian investigators and prosecutors have been documenting that damage — from the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam onwards — and building cases with no shared methodology to follow. That experience is now a tool others can use: the Manual on Prosecuting International Environmental Crimes, developed by Climate Counsel and UCLA’s The Promise Institute for Human Rights (Europe).

The Manual shows investigators, prosecutors and civil society how to build cases for serious environmental harm as international crimes — as war crimes where there is an armed conflict, and as crimes against humanity, which can be committed in peacetime.

At this event, co-organised by the Embassy of Ukraine in the Kingdom of the Netherlands and the Manual’s authors, the experts behind it will explain how it works, which crimes apply and how evidence is gathered, followed by an open discussion. The law already exists; this session is about using it. Whether you investigate, prosecute, research or campaign, or are simply curious how environmental destruction becomes a criminal case, you are welcome to join. No specialist background required.

events.title: Who Owns the Truth?
events.description:
Asymmetrical Haircuts, in partnership with Leiden University Centre for Peace and Justice, will host a live podcast exploring the intersections between history, memory and justice for serious human rights violations.
International justice mechanisms have been justified as contributing to truth, peace and reconciliation.  The “right to truth” for victims has been recognised and interpreted by different international courts and bodies. But the "truth" about conflicts, occupation and oppression is not just proof of the crimes in court. These are stories of families, communities and societies. So whose truth is it? Who owns it? And how do we preserve it?
Join us in the audience to hear expert practitioners from Bosnia and Herzegovina, The Gambia and Ukraine in the discussion.

events.title: What Does Gender Have to Do with It? Gender, the ICJ Judge, and the International Rule of Law
events.host: The City Law School, City St George's University, University of London, The Working Group on Gender Parity for the ICJ
events.description:
For 80 years, women judges have been a marked minority at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), and across its 80 years of jurisprudence, the Court has rarely engaged gender issues. Join us for an interactive evening dialogue exploring how a gender equal and gender engaged International Court of Justice is essential for the Court's legitimacy and in turn for the international rule of law.
The evening brings together diverse discussants and participants to focus on solutions to the ICJ's gender inequality and encourages all participants to commit to actions they can take to support a gender equal ICJ. We invite all participants to reflect on the relationships between the international rule of law, a representative international judiciary, and the mainstreaming of gender equality. 

🗓 Tuesday, 17 November 2026 | 🕤 5:15 pm-7:00 pm (CET)
📍 Leiden University, the Hague Campus, Wijnhaven Building, Room 3.48, Turfmarkt 99, 2511 DP The Hague, Netherlands | Zoom Link 

Attending in person? Please join us for the drinks and nibbles reception following the discussion.

events.title: No Peace Without Justice: Survivor Voices and Accountability for Crimes in Ukraine
events.host: Netherlands Helsinki Committee, Eastern Ukrainian Centre for Civil Initiatives (EUCCI), Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Embassy of Switzerland to The Netherlands
events.description:
Peace is not the absence of war, but the presence of justice. Justice has a different meaning for each survivor. It is therefore crucial that the stories of survivors are heard and understood as part of the broader accountability process. As part of The Hague Justice Week on 17 November 2026, the Netherlands Helsinki Committee (NHC) and the Eastern Ukrainian Centre for Civil Initiatives (EUCCI) are organising a discussion on accountability for crimes committed in Ukraine, as part of the project "Justice and Accountability for Ukraine: Strengthening the Role of Survivor- and Civil-Society-Led Initiatives", which is funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands. Held under the theme “80 Years and Beyond: Renewing the Promise of Peace and Justice Through Law”, this panel discussion will combine lived experience and legal expertise, aiming to facilitate a productive discussion centred on the needs of victims and the practical steps towards achieving justice.

 
About the Speakers
- Three survivors from Ukraine who lived under the occupation will share their stories: Maryna Suprun, Valentyna Pestushko and Volodymyr Scherbachenko (Executive Director - EUCCI). They will be joined by Dr Iva Vukušić, an Assistant Professor at the Utrecht University and an international expert on accountability for mass atrocities. She has over 10 years' experience working at war crimes tribunals and advising governments on accountability for crimes committed in Ukraine. Additionally, a representative from the Register of Damage for Ukraine (RD4U) will join the discussion to provide an institutional perspective on justice opportunities for victims.
The discussion will be moderated by Céline Guyénot (Programme Officer – Netherlands Helsinki Committee).

 
Stories from Life Under Occupation

EUCCI will present “Uninvited”, a book compiling 25 personal stories from Ukrainians who lived under Russian occupation between 2014 and 2022. Contributions from residents of the Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Kherson and Chernihiv regions describe the human rights violations they suffered, such as ''violations of basic freedoms, physical threats, lack of access to water, food, medical care and information, and homes that became places of confinement".Peace is not the absence of war, but the presence of justice. Justice has a different meaning for each survivor. It is therefore crucial that the stories of survivors are heard and understood as part of the broader accountability process. 


Event details:

Time: 17:00-19:30 

 Venue: Bankhall, Het Nutshuis. Riviervismarkt 5, 2513 AM The Hague, Netherlands

events.title: The Hague Justice Week Networking Breakfast
events.description: This networking breakfast, hosted at The Hague Humanity Hub, is one of the official networking moments of The Hague Justice Week. Over coffee and breakfast, participants, speakers, practitioners, researchers and advocates are warmly invited to come together before the day’s programme begins. It’s a relaxed opportunity to share highlights from the week so far and connect with others working on peace, justice, human rights and international cooperation.

events.title: Safeguarding women and girls’ rights in digital spaces: Unpacking rule of law approaches to address online violence against women and girls
events.host: International Development Law Organisation (IDLO), Embassy of Australia, The Philippines and the United Kingdom, The Hague Municipality and International Gender Champions
events.description:
The digital transformation of our daily realities is giving rise to new forms of online violence against women and girls (VAWG). Although the pattern and forms of online violence are unique, they are part of a continuum of violence and discrimination experienced offline, reinforcing systemic inequalities against women and girls. Globally, law and policymakers continue to struggle to comprehensively address online VAWG, leaving significant gaps in legal frameworks for survivors to seek protection or access justice. Even when laws are in place, law enforcement personnel or judiciaries often lack the skills and knowledge, or technical expertise to effectively prevent, respond or adjudicate. This event will bring together policymakers, experts, private sector and civil society to explore the key legal and justice challenges in preventing and responding to online violence.
Furthermore, panelists will discuss current and future initiatives aimed at eliminating online VAWG, in line with the UN 16 Days of Activism against Gender Based Violence Campaign, starting on 25 November 2026.

events.title: When Discomfort Becomes Dialogue: Practising Relational Justice
events.host: The Hague University of Applied Sciences (THUAS)
events.venue: The Hague University of Applied Sciences
events.description:
In this highly interactive, innovative, and critical dialogue session, participants are invited to co-create and enact a case that brings together different bodies of law, the emotional dimensions of formal rules and regulations, and questions of social justice. The goal is to foster a moment of “emotional reflexivity” among people from diverse positionalities, where discomfort is embraced as an opportunity for relational learning.

We will draw on frameworks developed through the Relational Peer Mediation project currently underway at The Hague University of Applied Sciences. These include the pedagogy of discomfort, Theatre of the Oppressed, and the Comenius-inspired concept of relational peer mediation. The session is designed for students, educators, and researchers seeking to develop alternative ways of relating within educational contexts.

events.title: The Consensus Trap:  Why Governance Organisations Cannot Decide and What to Do About It
events.description:
Most governance organisations are genuinely committed to hearing from the people they serve. They consult widely, run surveys, hold roundtables, and invest in participation. And then, somehow, still cannot decide.

This session is about that gap, the space between consultation and action that quietly undermines trust, wastes resources, and leaves the people who were consulted feeling unheard despite having been asked.

“The Consultation Trap” brings together practitioners from governance, international justice, and social design to examine why organisations that do everything right on paper still get stuck. We look at the structural and relational dynamics that turn consultation into delay, and what it actually takes to build decision processes that move without sacrificing the legitimacy that participation is supposed to create.

Participants can expect a candid, practitioner-led conversation grounded in real cases and lived experience. This is not a lecture. It is a working session for people who sit inside these systems and want honest tools, not more frameworks. The panel includes voices from international justice innovation, governance strategy, and organisational change, and the format is designed to create space for the room to contribute, not just listen.

You should attend if you work in or alongside governance organisations, public institutions, NGOs, international bodies, civil society, and have ever left a meeting wondering how a room full of capable people managed to agree on nothing. This session is for you.

events.title: Scaling People-Centred Justice with AI
events.venue: Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) office
events.description:
Millions of people across Africa first encounter the justice system not in a courtroom, but at a police station, a checkpoint, or through a phone screen. In Nigeria alone, an estimated 25 million people face legal problems every year, and more than 14 million cannot get the help they need. AI-powered tools are opening new possibilities for delivering legal information, guidance and support at scale and closer to the point of need but scaling them responsibly raises real questions about reliability, privacy, bias, accountability and human oversight.

This interactive session brings together experiences from Nigeria (Justice Padi AI), Tunisia and Niger with justice practitioners, policymakers and technology partners to explore what these emerging models teach us about expanding access to justice across different legal, institutional and infrastructure contexts. Participants will hear a moderated panel discussion and country snapshots, then step into the "From Prototype to Scale-Up" simulation, a board game in which teams take on the role of decision-makers deploying an AI-powered justice solution, navigating real dilemmas around data governance, ethics, institutional resistance, financing and political constraints.

Come for a candid look at what it really takes to move AI-for-justice tools from prototype to sustainable scale, and leave with practical considerations for responsible design, human oversight and institutional collaboration.

events.title: One World, One Home, One Law for All: Commemoration Centenary ICJ Judge and Vice-President Christopher Weeramantry (17.11.1926)
events.host: Judicap in co-operation with Sri Lanka Embassy
events.description: Even a century after the establishment of the World Court in 1920, one of the greatest challenges facing international law remains that of bringing the world’s diverse cultures and legal traditions into harmony. Several judges have made exceptional contributions to this endeavour. A prominent figure in recent decades was Christopher Weeramantry of Sri Lanka (ICJ judge, 1991–2000). Throughout his life, he sought common ground among the world’s major religions and emphasized the moral convictions that unite humanity. His principled position in the 1996 advisory proceedings on the legality of the threat or use of nuclear weapons remains as relevant as ever. At the gathering at the Embassy of Sri Lanka, the judge’s former colleagues and students will discuss the significance and feasibility of Weeramantry’s ideas in an era of growing polarisation and the erosion of international law.

events.title: Arrest Warrants and Peace Negotiations: Charting New Pathways Towards Peace and Justice
events.venue: Leiden University, Campus Spui, Spui 5, 2511 BL Den Haag
events.description:
International criminal justice is increasingly relevant in situations of ongoing conflict or conflict transformation. At the same time, the dynamics and formats of peace negotiations are rapidly evolving in times of changing geopolitics. 
These developments pose challenges in relation to the interplay of peace and justice. How can states simultaneously uphold their legal obligations to investigate and prosecute international crimes and cooperate with international legal institutions, such as the International Criminal Court (ICC), while facilitating negotiations aimed at ending armed conflict and reaching long term sustainable peace? 
What legal and practical avenues exist to reconcile peace and justice, without prioritizing one over the other? What space does the law of cooperation provide for consultation or diplomatic initiatives? 
If you are interested in these discussions, join us for our expert seminar and debate on Arrest Warrants and Peace Negotiations: Charting New Pathways Towards Peace and Justice

events.title: Civic Actors Between Authoritarianism and International Power
events.host: Democracy and Rule of Law Collective, World Liberty Congress, Lex Populi
events.description:
What happens when the people working hardest to defend democracy at home are caught between the authoritarian or illiberal governments they oppose and the international actors who claim to support them? This session, organized in partnership between the Democracy & Rule of Law Collective, the World Liberty Congress and Lex Populi, brings together civic leaders, journalists, practitioners and researchers from different regions to explore exactly that question.  Rather than a traditional panel, this is a fishbowl discussion: a small group of speakers sits in a center circle and talks openly, while the audience sits around them and can rotate in to ask questions, respond, or join the conversation directly. Expect an informal, comparative exchange rather than a set of prepared remarks, drawing on speakers’ lived experience in Georgia, Kazakhstan, Nicaragua, Rwanda and China, with voices speaking both from exile and from within their home country. Everyone in the room is invited to explore similarities across these different contexts.

Together, we’ll examine who gets to shape democratic change, how international support can strengthen or sometimes complicate local efforts, and how civic actors can secure a meaningful role in decisions affecting their countries’ political futures.

Meet the Speakers: 

- Natacha Abingeneye: Civic organizer, human rights activist and social entrepreneur, and former President of Jambo ASBL, a diaspora-led organization working on human rights, justice and reconciliation in the Great Lakes region.
- Botagoz "Bota" Jardemalie (Kazakhstan): Human rights lawyer and Harvard Law graduate who has defended political dissidents for over a decade and advocates before the UN and the European Parliament.
- Wu'er Kaixi (China/Taiwan): Dissident and democracy activist, a leader of the 1989 Tiananmen student movement, and General Secretary of the Taiwan Parliamentary Human Rights Commission.
- Alexa Zamora (Nicaragua): Political activist with over a decade of experience advocating for democracy and human rights through international protection mechanisms, and recipient of the Martin Luther King Award for Democracy and Human Rights.
- Nino Dolidze (Georgia): Election integrity expert known for her leadership of the election watchdog ISFED, with two decades of democracy-building experience and recipient of the Madeleine K. Albright Democracy Award.

Whether you work in civil society, policy, journalism, or research, you’ll leave with a sharper, more grounded understanding of these dynamics than any single country’s story can offer on its own, along with practical lessons for building more inclusive approaches to democracy, justice, accountability and the rule of law. We warmly invite you to join the conversation, not just to listen.

events.title: Prevention at 80: The ICJ, the Duty to Prevent, and the Structural Limits of Anticipatory Justice
events.host: American Bar Association Center for Human Rights, Stichting ABA ROLI Netherlands
events.description:
Can international law stop a genocide before it happens, rather than judge it afterward? In 2007, in Bosnia v. Serbia, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that a state’s duty to prevent genocide begins the moment it learns, or should have known, of a serious risk of atrocity. Today that standard is being tested as never before, in Gambia v. Myanmar, South Africa v. Israel and Ukraine v. Russia, yet the gap between what the doctrine promises and what it achieves has never been wider.

Marking the Court’s 80th anniversary, this session asks whether the ICJ has built a genuine system of anticipatory justice or a vocabulary that arrives, structurally, too late. A moderated panel of experts will develop, rather than resolve, six tensions: how early a warning must be before the “should have known” duty kicks in; who can be expected to act, from third states to armed groups that control no territory; the limits of the Court’s reach when atrocity risk sits inside a single state at civil war; how well states actually observe the Court’s emergency orders (its Article 41 provisional measures); what happens when the Court allocates duties it cannot enforce while the UN Security Council stays deadlocked; and whether the recent surge of cases brought in the common interest strengthens deterrence or exposes how hard the law is to enforce. In this moderated webinar, expert panelists will examine what the law can and cannot do when prevention matters most.

events.title: Legal Clinic for Civil Societal Organizations
events.description:
During The Hague Justice Week, Partos and Pro Bono Connect are inviting civil society organisations to seek accessible legal advice from solicitors at various law firms.

Would you like to find out more about what a lawyer does, or would you like to ask for some advice? Do come along!

events.title: Judging International Justice - featuring Judge Hilary Charlesworth of the International Court of Justice, in conversation with Professor Anna Spain Bradley of UCLA Law
events.host: UCLA Law's The Promise Institute for Human Rights (Europe)
events.description: Join us for this annual event featuring Judge Hilary Charlesworth of the International Court of Justice in discussion with Professor Anna Spain Bradley, MacArthur Foundation Chair in International Justice and Human Rights at UCLA School of Law. The discussion will center on the evolving role of international adjudication and international law in the world today. This lecture series furthers the mission of The Promise Institute and UCLA by supporting public education and engagement with international justice and human rights.

events.title: Verhalenhuis Workshop Series
events.description:
Het Verhalenhuis offers storytelling workshops to people who have often had no prior contact with the performing arts and whose stories are underrepresented in society's mainstream narrative. Each Verhalenhuis edition consists of a series of 6-8 weekly workshops in which participants work on structuring stories and using body language and voice when sharing them.

During the Hague Justice week we are having a kick off for a new group in the Hague Humanity Hub together with Pitztop. The session is meant for 8-10 newcomers who want to get acquainted with theatermaking and storytelling. 

The skills to tell and present your own story are applicable in almost any field and can contribute to self-confidence and the sense that your story matters. By reclaiming stories under the motto "your story on your terms," participants discover the power of narrative in their own hands. Alongside the workshops, Het Verhalenhuis also offers these stories and storytellers a stage as a follow-up trajectory. Participants in the Verhalenhuis editions are invited to create a theatre production together with theatre-maker Arvand Dashtaray and the Virgule FPAC team. ROSE Stories also curates a digital version of Het Verhalenhuis, where participants can share their stories in digital format.

events.title: The Latest Front in the Fight for Free Speech: Screening of the "The Librarians"
events.host: International Federation of Library Association and Institutions (IFLA)
events.venue: KB National Library of The Netherlands
events.description:
The Emmy Award-winning documentary The Librarians tells the story of a fast-moving new front in the fight between free speech on one side, and censorship on the other. Librarians have increasingly found themselves having to take up the role of defenders of intellectual freedom, in the face of organised campaigns set on preventing access to materials on topics they don't like - LGBTQ, critical race theory, gender equality and more. 

This is not just an American problem. In Europe too, governments and private movements alike have shown their readiness to question, challenge, hide and censor. Following the screening, an expert panel will be discussing the issues presented and what they mean our our side of the Atlantic. We will also be sharing more positive insights into how libraries are serving as places where the communities they serve can access legal information and opportnities to uphold their rights.

events.title: Jeune Fille, Droit et Souveraineté Économique en Afrique
events.host: Cameroon Ministry of Justice, Reknow Femmes D'Expertise
events.description: Bringing together young people, legal professionals, economic actors, civil society, and more, this session will examine the barriers that limit girls' ability to access and exercise their rights, as well as the role of the law in turning rights into real opportunities. Through expert perspectives, real life experiences, and candid discussions, participants will explore the connection between girls' empowerment, sustainable development, and economic sovereignty. Join us for this interactive session exploring how girls' access to rights can contribute to their individual and collective autonomy as well as Africa's broader economic sovereignty.

events.title: Justice in an Age of Authoritarianism
events.description:
Justice in an Age of Authoritarianism will explore how authoritarian governments use tools such as political imprisonment, politically motivated prosecutions, surveillance, forced exile, and transnational repression — when governments target critics and dissidents even beyond their own borders — to silence opposition and weaken democratic movements.

Bringing together activists, human rights defenders, and legal experts with direct experience of these tactics, the session will move from documenting patterns of repression to examining what meaningful accountability can look like in practice. Participants can expect a candid discussion about where existing justice mechanisms are working, where gaps remain, and how international institutions and civil society can respond more effectively.

This session is for anyone interested in the intersection of authoritarianism, human rights, and international justice, and in how accountability can better protect those working for freedom and democracy.

Moderated by:
Kate Gibson Barrister - Doughty Street Chambers

Participants:
Carine Kanimba – Rwanda 
Muhamadjon Kabirov – Tajikistan
Wu’er Kaixi – China
Natalia Pelevina – Russia
Kiele Cabrera – Cuba

events.title: Not Just Upheld, Reimagined: Seeing Children as Children in International Law
events.host: Save The Children, Global Rights Compliance
events.venue: Save The Children, Laan van Nieuwe-Oost India, 131, 2593 Den Haag
events.description:
Children deserve protection, support, and accountability for violations of international law committed against them. This roundtable session will draw on Save the Children and Global Rights Compliance’s experiences in settings like Ukraine, Sudan, and OPT to frame a discussion around how to reimagine how international law and justice mechanisms see and protect children.
We encourage organizations, experts and activists working in the fields of international law and justice to join the discussion to re-center children in international law.

Background
Children are disproportionately impacted by armed conflict and international crimes, bearing the brunt of the effects of those crimes earlier, more intensely, and longer than adults. As conflicts around the globe intensify, children are faced with growing threats to their safety and wellbeing: attacks on their safe spaces, deportation, recruitment, violence and abuse, evolving weapons systems.

Despite the protections that are afforded to children under international law, enforcing these protections and holding perpetrators of violations of international law against children accountable remains limited. Children are uniquely vulnerable to harms from these violations: they are more likely to be injured by explosive weapons, they are more susceptible to indoctrination and family separation, and, after violations take place, they have the least access to processes that can offer them justice or remedy.

Children deserve protection, support, and accountability. This session will draw on Save the Children and Global Rights Compliance’s experiences in settings like Ukraine, Sudan, and OPT to frame a discussion around how to reimagine how international law and justice mechanisms see and protect children.

Speakers:
-        Dr. Jessice Hazelwood, Senior Legal Advisor, Save the Children
-        Ruby Mae Axelson, Gender and Child Justice Lead, Global Rights Compliance

events.title: The Hague’s International Zone: A Journey from War to Peace
events.description: This 2-hour walking tour takes you through The Hague’s International Zone, home to many of the world’s leading international organizations. Along the way, you will discover how this area transformed from a wartime landscape into a symbol of peace, justice, and international cooperation. Through its landmarks, institutions, and stories, the walk reveals how The Hague became known around the world as the International City of Peace and Justice.

events.title: Film Screening: Surviving Genocide – The Rohingya Quest for Justice
events.description:
A screening of a documentary movie, featuring victims and witnesses’ stories and their role in international justice process – and what it means to them and their community. The screening will be followed by a discussion about the first genocide case in decades and potential outcome and the role of victims and witnesses. The documentary focuses on the realities and significance of having victim voices before the International Court of Justice (ICJ). The discussion will also broadly highlight the positive impact of international law at a time that international law and justice institutions are under attack.

This short and poignant documentary offers a unique window into what international legal proceedings mean in practice for the people they are designed to serve. Looking into both technical and humane aspects, the film highlights the importance of the full inclusion of victims in legal processes. It shows what can be achieved when frontline organisations work hand in hand with UN mechanisms and states to support the most vulnerable people. Moving between the front and back stages of the first genocide case in nearly two decades, “Surviving Genocide – The Rohingya Quest for Justice” is a powerful testament to hope and the impact of collective action against hatred and impunity.

events.title: Roundtable on International Court of Justice (ICJ) Jurisprudence
events.host: Columbia Society of International Law & Columbia Journal of Transnational Law
events.description: Hosted by the Columbia Society of International Law and the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law, the session brings together two professors of international law and a group of Columbia Law students and looks at specific ICJ decisions and the questions scholars have not yet fully answered about them.

events.title: The Proposal for an International Anti-Corruption Court: Renewing the Promise of Justice, 80 Years On
events.host: Integrity Initiatives International Europe - III Europe
events.description:
Eighty years ago, the International Court of Justice (CIJ) opened in The Hague to settle disputes between countries. In the decades since, the international community has built new courts to hold individuals accountable for the gravest crimes, from war crimes to genocide. But one crime that does enormous damage still has no international court: grand corruption. Grand corruption, the theft of public money by those at the very top of government, drains hundreds of billions from public budgets every year, funds repression, and erodes people's trust in the institutions meant to protect them. Yet when national courts are unwilling or unable to act, there is often nowhere else to turn.

This session explores a proposal to change that: an International Anti-Corruption Court (IACC), a new court that would hold senior officials criminally accountable and help return stolen assets to the people they were taken from.
You'll hear from a senior official of the International Court of Justice, who will introduce the proposal and reflect on lessons from the Court's 80 years of experience; a former international criminal prosecutor who helped draft the treaty for the IACC; and two human rights defenders who have challenged authoritarian governments in Myanmar and Russia, who will explain how corruption keeps such regimes in power and what real accountability could mean for people on the ground. A moderator from The Hague municipality will guide the conversation, asking why this matters for the city and for governments elsewhere.

he panel will be followed by an open Q&A. Join us for a lively, accessible conversation about how justice can keep pace with the challenges of our time

events.title: Justice in New Languages: Youth, Art, and the Future of the Fight Against Impunity
events.venue: Pulchri Studio, Lange Voorhout 15, The Hague, Netherlands
events.description:
Eighty years after the founding of the International Court of Justice, a new generation is reimagining how communities pursue truth, accountability, and justice.

Across Kenya, Lebanon, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia, and beyond, young activists and community leaders are challenging impunity and confronting legacies of conflict and repression. Rather than relying solely on traditional legal and institutional approaches, they are using art, film, music, digital storytelling, and grassroots initiatives to make justice more accessible, meaningful, and relevant to their communities.

Organized by the International Center for Transitional Justice (ICTJ), this event will bring together young leaders and activists from different regions to share their experiences and explore how creative expression and community engagement can transform the pursuit of justice.

Through personal testimonies, multimedia presentations, and a moderated discussion, participants will discover how young people are finding new ways to address past injustices, preserve memory, and mobilize their communities. The programme will feature examples of creative initiatives, including photos and animated short film developed with Syrian and Sudanese civil society organizations.

The conversation will explore what international justice institutions can learn from these emerging approaches and how younger generations are helping shape the future of peace, justice, and accountability.

Following the discussion, guests are invited to a networking reception featuring an exhibition of artworks, photography, textiles, and other creative works developed through ICTJ's collaborations with communities affected by conflict and injustice.

Join us for an evening of dialogue, creativity, and connection celebrating the voices and ideas that are shaping the future of justice.

events.title: The Future of the Rule of Law in times of Crisis and Conflict
events.host: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), International Development Law Organization (IDLO), Hague Institute for Innovation of law (HiiL)
events.description:
Let’s look back in order to look forward. A promise made 80 years ago – to put law before force – must hold. 

With conflicts multiplying and justice out of reach for millions, how do we prevent crises, renew legitimacy and build justice and security systems that are people-centred, accountable and grounded in human rights?  

Join a conversation with judges, policymakers and civil society leaders to identify new solutions for new realities. The discussion will bridge international law and national justice systems with the lived realities of people and communities. You will hear voices from conflict zones, courtrooms and the institutions where the international justice agenda is shaped.
  
Challenge assumptions, hear different perspectives and help shape what stronger, more people-centred justice and rule of law can look like.

events.title: #DemocracyDrinks x The Hague Justice Week: Effects of a Shifting International Order
events.venue: Amare, Spinoza Room (1st floor), The Hague
events.description:
Join us for #DemocracyDrinks x The Hague Justice Week: Effects of a Shifting International Order

As the official networking event of The Hague Justice Week 2026, #DemocracyDrinks will bring the community together on 19 November for an evening of conversation, reflection and connection.

Eighty years after the foundations of the international legal order were laid, that order is shifting beneath us. What does the promise of peace and justice through law mean when the institutions built to protect it are under pressure? And what does this look like for people living with the consequences, sometimes far from the conference rooms where decisions are made?

Organised by The Hague Humanity Hub, the Netherlands Institute for Multiparty Democracy (NIMD), and the Netherlands Helsinki Committee (NHC), this special edition of #DemocracyDrinks will bring together people from across the international peace and justice ecosystem.

We will connect the big geopolitical picture to everyday lives, exploring how a changing global order is affecting democracy, international cooperation and the pursuit of justice. Speakers will be announced soon, but we can already promise an evening of thought-provoking conversations and new connections.

Bring your questions, meet others from across the ecosystem, and stay afterwards for drinks and good conversation.

events.title: Conscientious Lawyering: Realizing the Promise of International Law: International Humanitarian Law
events.description:
A series of panel discussions among leaders in the global legal profession about the role of lawyering in realizing the promise of international law.  Through seven (7) separate topical discussions held online during and after Hague Justice Week, attendees will be invited to consider how to develop their own pro bono or public interest practice in international law.  Specific areas of focus in international law are as follows:  
- International Lawyering 
- Artificial Intelligence Law

events.title: Mending the weave: Customary and informal pathways to lasting peace
events.host: European Forum for Restorative Justice (EFRJ),  International Development Law Organisation (IDLO), United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), EU Liaison Office to The Hague and Embassy of The Philippines
events.description:
In the 80 years since the International Court of Justice was established, customary and informal justice (CIJ) systems have become increasingly recognized for their role in the architecture of international peace and justice. When aligned with human rights standards and meaningfully connected to formal justice institutions, CIJ systems can contribute to preventing and resolving disputes, restoring trust and strengthening the rule of law, as well as promoting accountability and offering redress for violations of human rights and humanitarian law. As international justice institutions face crises of credibility and legitimacy around the world, there is a distinct role for community-owned, culturally- resonant pathways to justice. The challenge of engaging with CIJ systems is understanding how to do so in a manner that fosters coherence with formal institutions while safeguarding rights, particularly for women, youth, and marginalized and excluded groups.
This event will bring together practitioners, scholars, judicial actors, traditional and Indigenous leaders, and policymakers who can speak to how CIJ systems can strengthen access to justice, advance transitional justice, and sustain peace, in ways that are rights-based, gender-responsive, and restorative. It will also explore how to enhance the legitimacy of CIJ mechanisms in the eyes of the communities it serves.

events.title:
Legal Alternatives to War (LAW not War): 
Toward the universality and effectiveness of the ICJ at 80 years and beyond
events.host: World Federalist Movement, Institute for Global Policy
events.description:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) was established as the principal judicial organ of the United Nations to assist in the peaceful resolution of international disputes, and to strengthen and uphold the rule of law globally. The authority of the ICJ has contributed to a very good track record, resulting in compliance with the vast majority of its decisions. 
 However, the role of the ICJ is limited by the fact that its jurisdiction in contentious cases is based on mutual consent for a specific dispute, compromissory clauses in treaties or general acceptance of ICJ compulsory jurisdiction. 75 States currently accept ICJ compulsory jurisdiction. 
In this roundtable we will explore the value of advisory opinions and contentious cases, their complementarity and inter-play, why further acceptance of ICJ compulsory jurisdiction leading towards universality is important, and how to address potential concerns in accepting ICJ jurisdiction.

events.title: The Kosovo Specialist Chambers - History, Mandate and Proceedings
events.description:
This interactive in-person session provides information on the mandate and activities of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers which is a temporary court based in The Hague dealing with war crimes and crimes against humanity in Kosovo 1998-2000. It further elaborates how a relocated court bridges the distance in time and place to deliver justice.  

Participants will also be provided a tour of the public areas of the court.

events.title: Beyond the Rescue: Confronting Barriers to Justice for Child Survivors
events.description:
This session will unpack the often-hidden realities of the legal maze that child survivors of sexual abuse and trafficking face long after their initial rescue. Because dramatic rescue operations frequently capture public attention while the subsequent judicial hurdles remain largely invisible, this session, drawing from research conducted by Free A Girl in four countries, will focus on the systemic, procedural, and social barriers that obstruct true access to justice. The talk will highlight how the very institutions designed to protect vulnerable children often become secondary sources of trauma due to severe gaps in procedural rights, a lack of trauma-sensitive procedures, and inadequate witness protection.
This presentation will translate complex judicial failings and data into a deeply human narrative. Specifically, the session will aim to:
●        Highlight the intense financial, emotional, and social hurdles that will follow during the legal process.
●        Outline the specific barriers survivors encounter, including direct intimidation from perpetrators, social stigma, and the systemic failures.
●        Equip the audience with an understanding of the reforms required that will be necessary to transform a retraumatizing legal system into a genuine pathway for healing and restitution.

events.title: Colombia in Search of Justice - Relational Restorative Justice and the Comuneros del Sur Process in Nariño
events.host: Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Colombia
events.description:
The event takes the former Comuneros del Sur peace process in Nariño, south-western Colombia, as a concrete case through which to explore where justice is located in contexts of conflict and transition, and how formal, international, territorial, customary, and community-based approaches can work alongside one another to produce meaningful justice outcomes. The territorial negotiation formed part of the previous government’s ‘Total Peace’ policy. The Dutch Embassy in Bogotá accompanied the process as an international observer. 

The event aims at opening a wider conversation about the location, ownership, and practice of justice. The proposed event will bring together 30–40 invited participants with experience in international, criminal, transitional, restorative, customary, and community-based justice. The session will begin with short reflections from individuals directly involved in the Comuneros del Sur process, outlining how it developed, how relational restorative justice informed its architecture and practice, what tangible outcomes it achieved, and what its subsequent closure reveals about the possibilities and vulnerabilities of justice-making during conflict transition.

•        What does the Comuneros del Sur experience tell us about where justice is located and who should participate in defining and delivering it during conflict transition?
•        How can formal criminal justice, international standards, and territorial, indigenous, customary, and community-based justice practices connect constructively without one displacing the others?
•        What can the tangible outcomes achieved in Nariño teach us about pursuing justice in action during a peace process, and what lessons might this offer for peace and justice processes elsewhere?

After these initial brief interventions, the discussion will be opened to participants for questions, reflections, and exchange. The intention is to create a genuinely interactive conversation rather than a conventional panel discussion, drawing on the experience in the room to test what the Nariño case contributes to wider debates about complementarity, legal pluralism, people-centered justice, and the relationship between local practice and international justice. Where appropriate, participants from international justice institutions will be invited to respond to what the case might mean for their own understanding of justice and complementarity.

events.title: Peace Through People-Centered Justice: Renewing the Promise of Peace and Justice Beyond the Courtroom
events.host: Pathfinders, Government of the Netherlands, Embassy of the Republic of Guatemala to the Netherlands, Municipality of the Hague, Cordaid, and UNDP
events.description:
International efforts to advance peace and justice have traditionally focused on strengthening institutions, developing legal frameworks, and preventing or resolving conflict. Yet for most people, peace and justice are experienced much closer to home: in whether they feel safe in their communities, can resolve disputes fairly, and have access to justice when they need it. People-centered justice and violence prevention offer complementary approaches to addressing the grievances, exclusion, and unmet justice needs that can undermine trust and contribute to violence. Through initiatives such as Peace in Our Cities (PiOC) and the Justice Action Coalition (JAC), Pathfinders for Peaceful, Just and Inclusive Societies works to connect these approaches across local, national, and global levels.

This session will explore how cities, local governments, and community actors are advancing locally led approaches that strengthen access to justice, safety, trust, and social cohesion. Drawing on practical experiences, the discussion will examine how addressing people's everyday justice needs and preventing violence can reinforce one another, while highlighting lessons that can inform national and international policies and commitments to peace and the rule of law.

Following the panelists' initial reflections, the conversation will open to participants for questions and exchange, creating an opportunity to explore how we can build and sustain peace and justice from the local level upward.

events.title: Nuremberg Academy Dialogue: The United Nations and the Nuremberg Principles
events.description:
To mark the 80th anniversary of the United Nations (UN) and the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, the International Nuremberg Principles Academy will convene a high-level webinar bringing together leading scholars and legal practitioners.

The second Nuremberg Academy Dialogue will examine the foundational role of the United Nations and the International Law Commission in formulating the Nuremberg Principles and consider how these principles still matter today. It will explore how the principles recognised following the Nuremberg trials have shaped international criminal law and continue to inform accountability efforts for core international crimes, alongside current developments in the field. 

Participants will hear from leading experts, including Ambassador David Scheffer, Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, Professor of Practice at Arizona State University and former US Ambassador-at-Large for War Crimes Issues, and Professor Dr Cécile Aptel, Principal Advisor, UN International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism on Syria, and Professor of Practice of International Law, The Fletcher School, Tufts University. Chaired by Dr Viviane Dittrich, Deputy Director of the International Nuremberg Principles Academy.

events.title: Renewing the Memories #1 - Blue Island Screening & Discussion
events.description:
Renewing the Memories #1 presents a screening of Blue Island (2022), directed by Chan Tze-woon. Blending documentary interviews with re-enactments, the film brings together the personal memories of different generations and connects them with key moments in Hong Kong’s history.
By revisiting experiences of political upheaval, resistance, migration and loss, the film asks how memories can be preserved and passed on when public narratives are being reshaped or erased. It invites us to consider remembrance as an essential part of the continuing pursuit of peace and justice.
After the screening, director Chan Tze-woon will join us online for a live Q&A and discussion.

events.title: ‘30 Years of the Death of Yugoslavia: A Generational Perspective’
events.host: The Hague University of Applied Sciences (THUAS)
events.venue: The Hague University of Applied Sciences
events.description: Join us as we look back at the BBC’s The Death of Yugoslavia documentary, 30 years later, and explore how the media, misinformation, and propaganda shaped the conflicts. We’ll also discuss how AI and social media have changed the way we receive and understand information today. Expect an interactive session with real-world examples, thought-provoking conversations, and open discussions where everyone is encouraged to share their thoughts. Whether you’re interested in history, politics, or modern technology, this is a great opportunity to explore how the past connects to the world we live in today!

events.title: Renewing the Memories #2 - The Taoyuan Airport Incident Screening & Discussion
events.description: Renewing the Memories #2 presents The Taoyuan Airport Incident (1986), filmed by Taiwan’s Green Team during the final years of martial law. Through this historical recording, the screening explores how independent images can challenge official narratives, preserve suppressed memories and contribute to the pursuit of democracy and justice.

events.title: Renewing the Memories #3 - Three Castrated Goats - Screening & Discussion
events.description: Set in rural Shaanxi during China’s strict COVID restrictions, "Three Castrated Goats" follows a man who returns home to collect three goats but becomes trapped by quarantine rules. Through dark humour and absurdity, the film reveals how systems of control enter everyday life and affect ordinary people. The film offers another perspective on censorship and the people responsible for enforcing it. Together, the two works invite reflection on freedom of expression, collective memory and life within systems of control. Director Ye Xingyu will join us online for a live Q&A after the screening.
